summary:
Workplace Insight reports that London has been ranked the world's most intelligent city in the inaugural Intelligent Cities Index from Boston Consulting Group (BCG). The index assessed 61 major cities across 39 countries against five measures of intelligent city maturity: resident outcomes, strategy, technology adoption, ways of working in government, and enabling factors such as infrastructure, talent and investment.

London topped the overall ranking ahead of Dubai, New York City, Washington DC and Amsterdam. The index is framed as measuring how effectively AI and digital tools improve daily life for residents and businesses rather than rewarding raw technology deployment. London scored particularly well on resident outcomes, including quality of life, employment opportunities and support for entrepreneurship.

BCG argues intelligent cities are distinguished less by new physical assets than by their ability to combine technology, governance and public services to produce better outcomes, which offsets criticism of London's ageing infrastructure. No single city dominates every dimension of digital maturity: Madrid ranked highest for strategic planning, Dubai led on technology adoption, New York topped government ways of working, and Amsterdam performed best on enabling conditions such as talent and investment.

For employers, the piece frames the findings as reinforcing London's attractiveness for knowledge-intensive industries despite housing costs, transport capacity and affordability concerns, citing a deep labour market, world-class universities, a strong technology ecosystem and widespread adoption of digital public services. BCG also challenges the assumption that only cities with heavy infrastructure investment can lead on AI, suggesting municipalities can improve resident outcomes by expanding AI-enabled public services while strengthening governance, data capabilities and digital skills.

The article closes with a takeaway for workplace strategists: successful cities will integrate technology with organisational change, skills development and effective public service delivery rather than treating AI as a standalone initiative.
